newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU steel producers launch complaint against U.S.
newsitem.headline: EU steel producers launch complaint against U.S.

text.p: European steel producers have asked the European Commission to press Washington to roll back decades-old U.S. legislation they say contravenes world trade rules.

EUROFER, the trade association of European iron and steel producers, said in a statement it had asked the Commission -- the EU's executive -- to seek the repeal of U.S. laws known as "the Antidumping Act of 1916".
The organisation said their complaint was in response to a suit filed in Utah on September 17 by U.S. company Geneva Steel Corporation against Germany's Thyssen Steel Group and others.

"The American steel industry's resort to this statutory relic is a prime example of the problem of harassment in the guise of trade law remedies," said Dietrich von Hulsen, director general of EUROFER.

"Before this new form of procedural protectionism harms our members' ability to deliver steel at fair, competitive prices to their American customers, we are asking the European Commission to exercise its rights under European and international law to seek the repeal of this outmoded statute," he said.

Geneva Steel is seeking $90 million in damages from Thyssen and a Houston-based importer Ranger Steel Supply Corp, accusing them of attempting to undermine the U.S. industry by selling underpriced plate imports from China, Russia and Ukraine.

In response to a complaint by Geneva Steel, the U.S. International Trade Commission said on December 18 that it had found "reasonable indication" American markets were being hurt by imported steel plate from these countries.
The ITC is due to release a final report on April 14 and the investigation could eventually lead to anti-dumping duties being imposed.
In its petition to the European Commission, EUROFER said it had identified "seven critical areas in which the 1916 Act contravenes World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules.
"The United States has long been the champion of developing an international system of rules to which all trading nations should adhere and be held accountable," Von Hulsen said.

"In this case it needs to put its own house in order ... and it should do so before other law-abiding exporters and importers are subject to the menace of huge legal fees and disruption to their legitimate business interests."

Under EU procedures, the Commission must decide within 45 days whether to launch a formal investigation into EUROFER's complaint. An investigation could take up to five months and lead to a dispute being lodged with the WTO.
